teach.title: A scene set beside the sentence
teach.say: Latin can give the circumstances of an action in two words: **the ablative absolute (a noun + participle set apart in the ablative: 'with X doing')**. *Sōle oriente nautae nāvigant* — with the sun rising, the sailors sail; in ordinary English, as the sun rises. The pair says when or why, and the main sentence goes on without needing it.

check.ask: Which two words give the circumstances rather than the main action?

teach.title: Both words ablative, and agreeing
teach.say: Both halves wear an ablative (the 'by/with/from' form) ending, and they agree in number: for one, *cane lātrante*, *magistrō recitante*; for more than one, *puerīs dormientibus*, *nautīs canentibus*. The participle (a verb used like an adjective) ends *-ante* or *-ente* in the singular, *-antibus* or *-entibus* in the plural.

check.ask: Puerīs dormientibus: what case and number is each of the two words?

teach.title: Loose from the rest of the sentence
teach.say: 'Absolute' means untied: neither word is the subject or the object of the main verb. In *Patre absente Mārcus in hortō lūdit* the one playing is Mārcus, not *patre*. Cover the pair with your hand — *Mārcus in hortō lūdit* is still a whole sentence, which proves the pair was scenery.

check.ask: Which two words can you cover and still be left with a whole sentence?

teach.title: It may come first or last
teach.say: The pair usually opens the sentence, but it can just as well follow: *Discipulī omnēs tacent magistrō intrante* means exactly what *Magistrō intrante discipulī omnēs tacent* means. Position is not what marks it; two agreeing ablatives, one of them a participle, are.

check.ask: This pair comes at the end. Which two words are they?

teach.title: One ablative, or two?
teach.say: A single ablative beside a verb is usually the ablative (the 'by/with/from' form) of the thing used: *gladiō pugnat*, he fights with a sword. An ablative absolute is two words that agree and one of them is a participle: *hostibus clāmantibus*. *Mīles gladiō pugnat, hostibus clāmantibus* carries both in one line — the sword is the tool, the shouting enemy the scene.

check.ask: One ablative here is the thing used; the other two words are the pair that sets the scene. Which two words are the pair?

teach.title: Present participle means at the same time
teach.say: The participle in this pair is present, so its action runs alongside the main verb, and the main verb fixes when that is: *Mēdō loquente Lȳdia tacet* — while Medus is speaking, now, Lydia is silent. Say 'as' or 'while' and keep the main verb's own time; 'with X doing' is right but stiff.

check.ask: Which two words say what is happening at the same moment as the sailors call out?

core.text: Latin can set a small scene beside the main sentence by putting a noun and a participle (a verb used like an adjective) together in the ablative: **the ablative absolute (a noun + participle set apart in the ablative: 'with X doing')**. *Sōle oriente nāvis ēgreditur* — with the sun rising, the ship goes out: as the sun rises. *Cane lātrante iānitor excitātur* — with the dog barking, the doorkeeper is woken. The pair stands loose ('absolute') from the rest: neither word is the subject or object of the main verb. Latin name: ablātīvus absolūtus.
English has the same thing, rarely: *weather permitting, we sail*. Usually we say *when the sun rose* — a clause with *when* or *while*.
Noun + present participle, both ablative, agreeing, not part of the main sentence = 'while / as X is doing'.

invented.en: While the teacher reads aloud, the pupils are silent.

core.text: *Gladiō pugnat* — one ablative, a thing used, no participle: the ablative (the 'by/with' form). An ablative absolute is two words agreeing, one a participle: *cane lātrante*. Test: drop the pair — is the rest still a complete sentence? *Iānitor excitātur* stands alone, so *cane lātrante* was extra scenery.

more.text: With a perfect participle (the 'having been done' word: laudatus = praised) the absolute says *after X was done*: *Ariadnā relictā* — Ariadne having been left, after leaving Ariadne. That is the next skill. The participle may even be missing, leaving noun + adjective or noun + noun: *lūnā plēnā* — under a full moon; *Caesare duce* — with Caesar as leader.

The noun in the absolute must not be the subject or object of the main clause; if it is, Latin uses a plain participle agreeing with it instead: *puer dormiēns gallum nōn audit*. And a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) gives an active-sense present participle: *sōle oriente*, from *orīrī*.

The learner's notes (week 16): a noun and a matching adjective — very often a participle — in the ablative give the circumstances in which the main action happens; there is no English equivalent, so translate with whatever conjunction fits: *pāstōre sub arbore dormiente, lupus venit* — as the shepherd sleeps under a tree, a wolf comes; *lūnā plēnā, mīlitēs fugiunt* — under a full moon; *nēmine vidente* — when nobody was watching. Ørberg brings it in in chapter XVI (*sōle oriente*, *multīs hominibus spectantibus*) without naming it; A&G §419–420 give the whole picture.
